checks.verdict: I planted seven new faults, one per scene, and measured them one at a time. All results are in <working folder>/checks/verify-new, checked with check_shot.py md5 06abffe677dac507df6d29e1afc0838a. The tool works well on three of them, the faults that change sizes or the camera. A lamp post running edge-to-edge along the board for 402 rows is not reported, and a false "chair touches lamp post" alarm is reported in its place. Some fixes would not work: the board-size fix puts the board where the chair and pail stand, and the barrel fixes give no distance. findings.where: paper-film/tools/check_shot.py check_pairs, lines 694-705 (depth measured on the whole-prop masks over 'showing = both & (visible[a] | visible[b])')
findings.evidence: Scene verify-new/k-lamp-post-touches-board, made with --break "gas-lamp-post:-0.53,0,0" (worked out so the post's right edge lands on the board's left edge, column 755). In ids.png the visible post edge runs within 2 px of the visible board edge for 402 rows, from about 0.44 to 0.65 down; see k-crop.jpg. The report never mentions lamp post with board. That pixel is on a collar of the post that sits behind the board, and no visible lamp-post pixel is within 5 px of it. The only fix in the report that happens to cure this is problem 3, a reference-matching item: 'Move lamp post about 0.35 m to the right'.
findings.fix: Judge an overlap only where the back prop's outline shows: measure depth in pixels of visible[back] next to visible[front], or measure row by row along the shared boundary. Flag any stretch longer than about 40 px where the two visible outlines are between 14 px overlapped and 18 px apart (a 0 px gap counts), even if some hidden part overlaps deeply elsewhere.

checks.verdict: The tool does most of its job. On the eight measured scenes its turn and tilt signs agree with Blender to within 0.4 px for every light and for where the lines meet. The camera-height, rule 1, rule 12 slide/turn and reference-size formulas check out (metres per pixel = distance/focal). Re-run with the current tool, all seven planted faults still come out as problem 1, except d, where the pail appears only at the end of problem 1's fix. But it gives wrong answers in cases close to the ones it was built for. A prop sunk into the pavement is called floating, and the fix says to lower it further. A prop just past the frame edge is called "hidden behind the set". The camera's lean (roll) has the opposite sign in the projection. A check file with no "lines" always fails rule 1. A landscape frame with the portrait reference gets "turn 16.3 degrees" as Fix first. Several checks can never fail: a prop up to 40% cut off at the bottom or left, a title zone given in pixels or with no area. Three unusual inputs crash it with a raw traceback.

findings.title: A prop sunk into the ground is reported as floating, and the fix says to lower it further
findings.where: shot_facts.py, the per-group loop (ray starts at low.z + 0.05, current line 214); check_shot.py check_resting (only air > 0.03 is checked, a negative value is never flagged)
findings.evidence: Measured with the current shot_facts.py (md5 157e2c30) using --break "wooden-pail:0,0,-0.10;brazier:0,0,-0.30", saved to $S/verify-code/m-sunk-2. The pail is sunk 0.10 m: its bottom is at 1.518 against the pavement at 1.618, yet facts say stands_above_surface_below = +0.072. The drum is sunk 0.30 m and reads +0.167. Report $S/verify-code/out3/m-sunk-2/report.md, problem 1: 'drum is floating: there is 0.17 m of air ... Fix: Lower drum by 0.17 m'. Problem 2: 'Lower pail by 0.07 m'. Cause: once the bottom is more than 5 cm below the surface, the ray starts underneath it and finds a surface lower down. A sink of under 5 cm reads as negative air and passes as 'within 3 cm'. The old shot_facts.py gave the same numbers ($S/verify-code/m-sunk).
findings.fix: In shot_facts.py, also cast a ray upward from low.z, up to the group's centre and ignoring its own parts. If it meets an upward-facing surface, record a negative stands_above_surface_below, meaning sunk by that much. Or cast downward from the group's top, ignoring its own parts and anything that rests on it. In check_resting, flag air < -0.03 as 'sunk X m: raise it X m'.

findings.title: A prop just past the frame edge is reported as 'in the frame but hidden behind the set'
findings.where: check_shot.py check_missing, the 'else' branch (hider = ... 'the set (a wall or a house)'); shot_facts.py screen_box_unclipped (a box from the 8 corners of each bounding box)
findings.evidence: Measured with --break "wooden-pail:0.50,0,0", saved to $S/verify-code/m-pail-just-out. The pail's solo picture has 0 pixels: it is wholly past the right edge. Report $S/verify-code/out3/m-pail-just-out/report.md, problem 1: 'pail is in the frame but hidden behind the set (a wall or a house). Fix: Move pail out from behind the set'. The bounding box sticks out past the outline (here by 0.026 of the width on the left), so this happens over a band of positions about 3 cm wide, not one exact spot.
findings.fix: In check_missing, test shot.alone[g].any() first. If the solo picture is empty, the prop is outside the frame: name the side from the box's centre or the edge it crosses, and give the move. Only call a prop hidden when its solo picture has pixels in the frame.

findings.title: The camera's lean (roll) has the opposite sign in check_shot's projection
findings.where: check_shot.py camera_axes (current line 422), used by project(), our_projection() and ground_point()
findings.evidence: Measured a camera leaned with Blender Euler Y = +5 degrees (my script $S/verify-code/roll_camera.py), saved to $S/verify-code/m-rolled; facts give roll_degrees 5.0. For 23 lights, check_shot.project() with that roll misses Blender's own on-screen positions by 25 to 1074 px. With the roll negated it matches to within 0.4 px (run against the copy check_shot.final-tested.py). Worked out directly: Euler Y = +5 moves the camera's right side down, (0.989, 0.119, -0.087), while camera_axes moves it up, (0.989, 0.119, +0.087); see $S/verify-code/roll_test.py. This only matters for a leaning camera, which rule 2 already flags. In that case two numbers come out wrong: where a floating out-of-frame prop lands once lowered (check_missing), and which warm lights light the marked patch (warm_lights_near).
findings.fix: In camera_axes, return right*cos(lean) - up*sin(lean) and up*cos(lean) + right*sin(lean), or write roll_degrees with the opposite sign in shot_facts.py. Then test it against the m-rolled lights.

findings.title: With no street lines in the check file, rule 1 always fails, as 'the camera faces down the street'

findings.title: A landscape frame is judged against the portrait reference's fractions: Fix first says turn 16.3 degrees while the camera match says ours matches
findings.where: check_shot.py check_reference_lines, check_reference_places, check_camera_match (scale = shot.width / size[0]); Shot.__init__ (check 'size' never compared with facts 'size'; picture silently resized)

When the shapes differ, skip the reference's lines_meet and boxes with a note, or redraw them through the matched camera. Scale pixel errors by the ratio of focal lengths, not widths. findings.title: The 'worst first' ranking compares numbers on different scales
findings.where: check_shot.py Report.rank and the how_bad of each check
findings.evidence: Rule 12's how_bad is right edge / limit, so even a prop well off the frame scores only about 1.1 to 1.6. In scene d the pail is 6% of the frame past the edge and scores 1.12. A 1-pixel rule-4 gap scores 17.58 (scene a: lamp post and winding wheels). 'Lit from below' scores 0.10/lift, which reached 5.29 in composed-end. Rule 3 'apart' scores 3 per prop, and rule 10 'outshines' is a flat 2. So which problem in tier 5 comes first depends on how each formula happens to scale, not on how far past its limit each one is. See the RANK lines from $S/verify-code/rank_dump_final.py.
findings.fix: Measure every how_bad the same way: how far past the limit as a share of the limit, e.g. (value - limit) / limit, capped, with the same direction for 'too much' and 'too little'. Or rank the composing rules in a fixed order.

findings.title: Rule 1's view-angle formula leaves out the camera's turn
findings.where: check_shot.py check_reference_lines (view = 2*atan(slope / (2*above)))
findings.evidence: For a level camera turned by yaw, the lines meet (slope / (2*tan(fov/2)*cos(yaw))) of the frame height above the middle. Putting composed-end's own numbers in (meet 0.43949 down, slope 0.069927, yaw 6.87 degrees), the formula gives 60.03 degrees for a camera whose true view is 60.4. Including cos(yaw) gives 60.40.
findings.fix: view = 2*atan(slope / (2*above*cos(radians(turn)))).

findings.title: 'Landed on something high' measures from a surface below the pavement, so its 0.5 m limit shifts from place to place
findings.where: shot_facts.py lowest_surface_below ('lowest' = the lowest upward-facing surface); check_shot.py check_resting (high > 0.5)
findings.evidence: composed-end facts: board, chair and pail stand on the pavement with 0.0 air, yet stands_above_ground is 0.179 to 0.183. The handcart on the road reads 0.366. So 'the ground' is a surface 0.18 to 0.37 m below the visible street, and a prop is flagged only when it is 0.13 to 0.32 m above the actual street.
findings.fix: Measure 'high' against the street's own height (the pavement or road model at that x, y, or y*tan(4 degrees) plus the kerb), not the lowest surface below.

checks.verdict: The reports catch every planted fault, and most fixes are given in metres. A non-programmer could follow "Fix first" alone only for a (camera too high), b (pail in the air), e (camera tilted) and f (drum standing apart). In c and g the lantern fix sends the lantern the wrong way. The fix for the notice's size, repeated in 7 reports, would make the notice too wide and push it further into the phone-button strip. The marks often fail the reader: the "Fix first" problem has no mark in 6 of the 8 scene reports, the lamp post's number sits beside the lantern, numbers are printed on top of each other in a, f and the old-picture report, and the old-picture report draws its boxes where the props are now, not where that older render shows them. Wording is mostly plain, but one thing often has two or three names (drum / fire / brazier_light; ground / pavement / surface / street; reference / "the picture the user liked"; turn), and some key words are never explained. Also, the stored reports b to g and old-picture were not made with the current check_shot.py: running it again on the same facts gives different numbers.

findings.title: c: the second fix option would sink the lantern 0.47 m into the chair seat
findings.where: c-chair-pushed-back-report/report.md, Fix first and problem 1; check_shot.py check_resting, line 564

Move the chair about 0.5 m towards the camera (down the street) so its seat is under the lantern again." In the code, work out the distance from the two middles (chair y 22.20, lantern y 21.68). Drop the 'lower it N m onto it' option, or base its height on the top of the seat rather than on the pavement.

findings.where: g-lantern-on-the-pavement-report/report.md, Fix first; check_shot.py line 569

In the code, work out the across, up-the-street and lift amounts from the chair's middle and seat height, and write 'seat', not 'top'.
